Subject: Connectivity planning for Redwood Private (on-prem)

Hi Evelyn,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Our architects want a short write-up on connectivity options so we can decide whether to go with a peering-style approach, use interface endpoints (PrivateLink), or run a site-to-site VPN into the private control plane. High level constraints: we expect sustained bursts up to 3k reqs/min, internal compliance requires egress controls, and we need the option for a failover path from a second colo.

I've attached our current network diagram. Can your team highlight tradeoffs (performance, ops complexity, security) and recommended guardrails for the pilot?

Cheers,
Alex
Sr. Cloud Architect, Telesto Health

From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Connectivity planning for Redwood Private (on-prem)

Alex — thanks for the diagram and context. Sharing a concise pros/cons summary below and a recommended pilot path. I'll follow with a one-page checklist for your NetOps team (attached).

Summary (short):
- VPC Peering: lowest latency, simple routing model, but limited cross-account controls and doesn't support private AWS-managed interface endpoints across accounts. Good if both sides can accept broad CIDR routing and you have direct inter-region connectivity needs.
- Interface endpoints (PrivateLink / endpoint services): strongest isolation (no route table changes), granular service-level controls, and easier to expose only the inference service. Slightly higher per-request latency and extra ops to manage ENIs and scaling. Better for regulated data-modes where minimizing lateral access is important.
- Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec): easiest to set up with existing NetOps, supports on-prem firewalls, but has variable throughput and higher jitter; requires HA pairs and often a second fiber/colo for reliable failover. Good as a fallback/DR path.

Pilot recommendation: Primary connectivity via PrivateLink (interface endpoints) + a secondary S2S VPN for failover and tooling (monitoring, health probes). Reserve VPC Peering only if your network team prefers full mesh network access and agrees to strict route filters.

Operational guardrails:
- Enforce least-privilege security groups and SG egress rules on the endpoint ENIs.
- Use mutual TLS between your inference clients and the service; don't rely solely on network-level controls.
- Provision monitoring on both paths (latency percentiles, token-level cost spikes).
- Limit CIDR ranges pushed to Redwood to minimal subnets (avoid /16 where possible).

I'll let Marcus and Karthik add notes on throughput and infra constraints. Attaching our on-prem checklist.

Thanks,
Evelyn Hart
Manager, Solutions Engineering — Redwood Inference

Adding throughput and HA considerations from the serving/runtime side.

- Throughput: PrivateLink introduces small CPU/ENI overhead; in our internal tests that adds ~3-8ms p50 overhead versus peering at equivalent packet sizes. For your burst target (3k reqs/min) this is negligible. If you plan sustained 10k+/min we should evaluate NAT/ENI scaling limits and consider dedicated cross-connects.
- Connection pooling: prefer keeping longer-lived connections from client to Redwood edge to amortize TLS and reduce cold-start latency. This is important for VPNs where re-establishing tunnels can be expensive.
- HA: If using VPN as primary, ensure two independent tunnels to different edge PoPs and test failover with route-preference modifications. If PrivateLink primary, configure health checks and automatic fallback to the VPN path on degraded latency/packet-loss.

Happy to run a quick perf pilot where we script 30m synthetic traffic across both paths and share p50/p95/p99.

—Marcus
Staff SRE, Redwood Inference

Alex — a couple of config nitty-gritty items from NetOps perspective that will speed onboarding: 

1) IP ranges: please provide one /28 for endpoint management and one service /27 for inference clients if possible. We can work with smaller ranges but routing and SGs are simpler this way.
2) MTU: confirm that site MTU >= 1400 to avoid fragmentation for model payloads; many IPsec tunnels default to smaller MTUs and that increases CPU/multipacket overhead.
3) SNI/ALPN expectations: if you plan to use our function-calling / stream features, make sure outbound SNI is permitted to the Redwood edge hostnames.

If you prefer peering instead of PrivateLink, we'll need a cross-account peering request and route table entries; that process typically adds a day or two to the onboarding timeline versus PrivateLink which can be issued by your NetOps team with a service consumer acceptance.

-Karthik
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
